mcqs.question: Why do some companies explicitly ask interviewers to note the quality of a candidate's questions on their feedback form?
options: It's a legal requirement in most hiring processes
The questions asked are a soft signal of genuine engagement and preparation, echoing the same competencies the rest of the loop measures
It's only used as a tiebreaker when two candidates score identically on everything else
It replaces the need for a dedicated behavioral round entirely
mcqs.explanation: A candidate's questions reveal how much homework they did and what they genuinely care about, which is itself a proxy for curiosity and ownership — the same things a behavioral round measures directly. There's no legal mandate for this, it isn't reserved purely as a tiebreaker, and it doesn't replace a dedicated behavioral round.

mcqs.question: You want to know what a strong first six months in the role looks like. Which interviewer should you ask, and why?
options: A peer engineer, since they experience day-to-day work most directly
Your prospective manager, since they're the one who defines and evaluates what a strong start actually looks like
A skip-level or director, since they set overall org strategy
It doesn't matter which interviewer you ask — any of them can answer this equally well
mcqs.explanation: A manager is the one actually setting expectations and evaluating performance, so they can answer concretely about what a strong start looks like — a peer would have a shallower, more anecdotal view, and a skip-level operates at a level removed from this specific evaluation. Matching the question to the role that owns the answer is exactly the point.

mcqs.question: Which of these is the strongest example of a signal-rich question to ask an interviewer?
options: "What's the culture like here?"
"Do you like working here?"
"What's the most painful piece of tech debt the team is currently living with?"
"What tech stack does the team use?"
mcqs.explanation: Asking about a specific pain point requires a real, concrete answer and gives you genuinely useful information about the job — the culture question is answerable identically anywhere, the "do you like it" question puts the interviewer on the spot with little information return, and the tech-stack question is usually already answerable from the job posting.

mcqs.question: An earlier interviewer mentioned the team is short-staffed on a specific project. What's the strongest way to use that later in the loop?
options: Ignore it, since questions should always be pre-written and unrelated to what happens during the loop
Bring it up only if an interviewer directly asks you to comment on team staffing
Repeat the exact same detail back to the same interviewer who mentioned it, to prove you were listening
Ask a later interviewer, such as the hiring manager, how that staffing gap affects the roadmap — showing you're synthesizing across the whole day
mcqs.explanation: Following up on an earlier detail with a different, well-positioned interviewer demonstrates active synthesis across the whole loop, which reads as more engaged than a purely pre-scripted question list. Ignoring it wastes a real opportunity, waiting to be asked defeats the purpose of showing initiative, and repeating it to the same person who said it doesn't add new value.

mcqs.question: A candidate says "no questions" at the end of every round to save time and let interviewers wrap up early. What's the actual effect?
options: It reads as disengagement and forfeits the loop's last opportunity to leave a positive impression
It's read as an efficient use of everyone's time and generally scores neutrally to positively
It has no effect on scoring since only the technical or behavioral rounds are actually graded
It's viewed positively as long as the candidate asked questions in at least one earlier round
mcqs.explanation: "No questions" reads as disengagement regardless of the polite intent behind it, and it wastes the final data point an interviewer forms their impression from — it isn't scored as neutral-to-positive efficiency, questions-asked can factor into feedback even outside a dedicated behavioral round, and one earlier good round doesn't offset repeatedly declining later.
